issues.title: Upgraded Q -> 3 from #839 [1698131435131]
totalWethDelegated does not decrease in withdraw can cause DOS
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L986-L987


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The accounting for total weth delegated increases when adding, but not withdrawing. This allows anyone to inflate this value by repeatedly adding and withdrawing. This again will cause DOS of the bonding mechanism.

## Proof of Concept

`RdpxV2Core.addToDelegate` increases `totalWethDelegated` while `RdpxV2Core.withdraw` does not decrease it:

```js
  function addToDelegate(
    uint256 _amount,
    uint256 _fee
  ) external returns (uint256) {
    ...
    // add amount to total weth delegated
    totalWethDelegated += _amount;
  }
```

This can be used to increase the value of `totalWethDelegated` through repeatedly adding and withdrawing. This value is used in `RdpxV2Core.sync` (which gets called in the bonding process) as part of a subtraction:

```js
balance = balance - totalWethDelegated;
```

This will cause an underflow and break the bonding.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Decrease `totalWethDelegated` when withdrawing


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L324
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L374
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L409
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1055
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1086


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Unauthorized contracts can bypass whitelistedContracts[msg.sender] due to EIP-2938.

## Proof of Concept
In the function `_isEligibleSender()` it checks `if (msg.sender != tx.origin){...}` but when EIP-2938 (a.k.a Account Abstraction) is fully implemented it will be possible to initiate transactions with contracts as they will be top-level accounts, just like EOAs. So the problem is when the function `_isEligibleSender()` checks if msg.sender != tx.origin all the txs initiated by non whitelisted contracts will be able to bypass it without reverting, the function is so sure no one can by pass it that it doesn't even revert (this is expected because at the moment contracts can't initiate txs).

The point is that when the tx.origin is a contract and can initiate txs it will be able to bypass  `whitelistedContracts[msg.sender]` without being whitelisted.

here it's the EIP for more information: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2938  (not necessarily this one but the core idea is in there, the idea of making contracts initiate tx is being implemented)


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1 - add revert logic for unauthorized contracts.
2 - Update _isEligibleSender() to account for EIP-2938 changes.









## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L790-L808


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The amount of ```reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance``` can be set to 0, by first calling ```addToDelegate()``` with the current value of ```reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance```, then calling ```withdraw()``` to withdraw all the deposited weth and then calling ```sync()```. When the admin of RdpxV2Core decides to call ```provideFunding()``` in order to send the funding amount of WETH to the PerpetualAtlanticVault contract, the function will revert, because ```reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance``` can be set to 0, and substracting the fundingAmount (whatever it is, if > 0) is not possible. The ```provideFunding()``` function is expected to be called at the end of every epoch as it can be called only once. The attacker can execute the above described flow and set ```reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance``` to 0 or close to 0 for example 6 days after the epoch has started (if 1 epoch is 7 days), or frontrun the ```provideFunding()``` function call. There is an ```emergencyWithdraw()``` function so the weth can eventually be withdrawn from the contract, but this is not the expected behavior. The attack will cost only the gas required for the three transactions, and as the intended chain for the Dopex protocol to be deployed is Arbitrum, gas will be pretty cheap.

I have added the below function in the RdpxV2Core contract in order to easily read the value of ```reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L315
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L201


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Any settle call can be reverted, thus disallowing the protocol from settling any options and from releasing the locked tokens.

## Proof of Concept

The protocol admin calls `settle()` on an option when its price gets bellow the strike price, at which the option is bought at. The issue arises due to a flawed check in `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.subtractLoss()`.

```solidity
require(
	collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss,
	"Not enough collateral was sent out"
);
```

This check makes front-running the transaction by donating 1 WEI for making it revert possible. 

Here is a Foundry PoC demonstrating the issue:

https://gist.github.com/CrisCodesCrap/d1e7af6ffec3abfe500949340c418577

## Tools Used

Manual review, Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider altering the check in the following way:

```solidity
require(
      collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) >= _totalCollateral - loss,
      "Some revert message here"
    );
```


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L258-L259
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L124-L136


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`reserveTokens` and `reserveAsset` are not synced because `reserveTokens` was not initialized in the constructor.

## Proof of Concept
The `RdpxV2Core.sol` contract stores the reserve token information and also uses another array to only track the reserve token symbols, the problem is that there is a mismatch since the constructor pushes a dummy `ZERO` token but it forgets to push its equivalent `reserveTokens` the value `ZERO`, so now when `addAssetTotokenReserves()` is called to add a new asset it pushes both `reserveAsset.push(asset)` and 
 `reserveTokens.push(_assetSymbol)`, so the current index of the former is 1 and the latter is 0, so there is a mismatch there.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add `reserveTokens.push("ZERO");` in the constructor right after the `reserveAsset.push(zeroAsset);` so both arrays are synced.



## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
As the `RdpxV2Core` contract burns RDPX tokens, a malicious attacker can benefit from a price manipulation attack using a flashloan attack

## Proof of Concept
The function `bond()` in the `RdpxV2Core` contract is a primary function to enter the protocol and bond DpxETH. This function accepts a `rdpxBondId` which if this parameter is equal to zero, then the `_transfer()` function switches the calculations from `RdpxDecayingBonds` token to `RDPX` ERC20 token. This function explicitly checks all the required criteria and it works well. However, this type of transfer for corresponding zero `bondId` is somehow similar to a fee-on-transfer mechanism. It burns a small portion of RDPX token and makes the RdpxV2 core contract makes the RDPX token inflation-proof. This burning mechanism can affect the RDPX token price if great DpxETH bonding amounts are passed to the `bond()` function.
Consider an attacker gets a large amount of WETH and swaps some portion of these tokens to RDPX tokens via the Uniswap v2 routers. Now the attacker has large WETH and RDPX balances. Then the attacker decides to call the `bond()` functions with proper amount of DpxETH bonding amounts. This will make the core contract burn some large amounts of RDPX. When an option is ITM, the admin can call the `settle` function of the RdpxV2Core contract, which will call the `settle` function of the PerpetualAtlanticVault contract. issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1189-L1190
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L576-L583


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Due to a lack of adequate precision, the calculated strike price for a PUT option for rDPX is not guaranteed to be 25% OTM, which breaks core assumptions around (1) protecting downside price movement of the rDPX which makes up part of the collateral for dpxETH & (2) not overpaying for PUT option protection.

More specifically, the price of rDPX as used in the `calculateBondCost` function of the RdpxV2Core contract is represented as ETH / rDPX, and is given in 8 decimals of precision. To calculate the strike price which is 25% OTM based on the current price, the logic calls the `roundUp` function on what is effectively 75% of the current spot rDPX price. The issue is with the `roundUp` function of the PerpetualAtlanticVault contract, which effectively imposes a minimum value of 1e6. 

Considering approximate recent market prices of $2000/ETH and $20/rDPX, the current price of rDPX in 8 decimals of precision would be exactly 1e6. Then to calculate the 25% OTM strike price, we would arrive at a strike price of `1e6 * 0.75 = 75e4`. The `roundUp` function will then round up this value to `1e6` as the strike price, and issue the PUT option using that invalid strike price. Obviously this strike price is not 25% OTM, and since its an ITM option, the premium imposed will be significantly higher. Additionally this does not match the implementation as outlined in the docs.

When a user calls the `bond` function of the RdpxV2Core contract, it will calculate the `rdpxRequired` and `wethRequired` required by the user in order to mint a specific `_amount` of dpxETH, which is calculated using the `calculateBondCost` function:

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L455-L462
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L515-L558


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `setSlippageTolerance` function in RdpxV2Core allows setting an unchecked slippage tolerance percentage. This is used in `_curveSwap` to calculate `minAmount` parameter, which can be exploited to drain funds.

## Vulnerability Details
The `setSlippageTolerance` function sets the `slippageTolerance` state variable without any upper bound:

```solidity
function setSlippageTolerance(uint256 _slippageTolerance) external onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) {

  require(_slippageTolerance > 0, "Zero slippage"); 
  
  slippageTolerance = _slippageTolerance;

}
```

This `slippageTolerance` is used in `_curveSwap` to calculate the `minAmount` parameter:

```solidity
function _curveSwap(uint256 _amount, bool _ethToDpxEth, bool validate, uint256 minAmount) internal returns (uint256 amountOut) {

  if(validate) {
    // minAmount calculation using slippageTolerance
    minAmount = _ethToDpxEth ? 
      ((_amount * getDpxEthPrice() / 1e8) - ((_amount * getDpxEthPrice() * slippageTolerance) / 1e16)) :
      ((_amount * getEthPrice() / 1e8) - ((_amount * getEthPrice() * slippageTolerance) / 1e16)) 
  }

  // Swap
  amountOut = curvePool.exchange(...)
}
```

By setting a high `slippageTolerance`, an attacker can set `minAmount` to an extremely low value and manipulate the swap price to drain funds.

## Impact

This vulnerability could lead to loss of user funds. With 100% slippage tolerance set, the loss could be up to 100% of swapped funds.

Here is a proof of concept demonstrating this attack on Kovan testnet:

1. Deploy the RdpxV2Core contract on Kovan

2. Call `setSlippageTolerance` with 10000000 (100% tolerance)

   RdpxV2Core.setSlipp

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L123-L125


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Users can get more shares than they should.

## Proof of Concept

Users can get more shares than they paid for because `vaultLp.deposit()`'s share calculation is done before the contract updates the funding token balances. This makes it so that users can deposit into the vault as if there isn't any new funding, but then update the funding in the line bellow.

```solidity
// @audit shares get calculated here:
require((shares = previewDeposit(assets)) != 0, "ZERO_SHARES");

// @audit Funding gets updated here, effectively allowing users to mint shares at old rates, but instantly get more value than they deposited.
perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding();
```

Consider the following PoC demonstrating the issue at hand:

https://gist.github.com/CrisCodesCrap/ab356eb14667dfe83b5ba1155b2ded4c

## Tools Used

Manual review + Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider calling `vault.updateFunding()` before doing the share calculation to fully mitigate the issue.

Here is how it may look like when implemented:

```solidity
// @audit First: the funding gets updated
perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding();

// @audit shares get calculated afterwards to ensure the bug is mitigated
require((shares = previewDeposit(assets)) != 0, "ZERO_SHARES");
```


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/e96aaa5ea21f11b29d828dbe2d0745974cd046ed/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L577-L579

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
RdpxV2Core::_stake() - Users will receive less receipt tokens(75% less) than they should receive, then during redemption only receive max 25% of their deposited funds back, due to a math error.

- The following internal/external/public functions are affected by this bug:
_bondWithDelegate(), bondWithDelegate(), bond().

The total number of minted `receiptTokens` as well as the value of `receiptTokenAmount`(on L578 in the _stake() function) will be much less(4x lower/less) than it should be, due to math errors.

Since the RdpxV2ReceiptToken contract is out of scope for this audit contest, the bug there might be out of scope too?, but I will mention it below, because it affects the correctness of the in scope contract (state) due to this bug:

In the RdpxV2ReceiptToken contract, the _mint() on L31 inside the deposit() function is dividing _amount by 2. 
This is where it causes the amount of receipt tokens minted to be 4x less than it should be. 
(But regardless of whether its exactly 4x or not, it cannot be correct).

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L201


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
```solidity
  function subtractLoss(uint256 loss) public onlyPerpVault {
    require(
      collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss,
      "Not enough collateral was sent out"
    );
    _totalCollateral -= loss;
  }
```
If collateral token balance is not equal to `_totalCollateral - loss`, it will revert. 
`_totalCollateral` is a state variable that can be updated using `deposit`/`withdraw` or by vault. Parameter `loss` is calculated in `PerpetualAtlanticVault::settle` from options.
These variables cannot be controlled directly and the protocol assumes collateral token balance of the contract strictly follows rules.
Malicious actor can break the assumption and grieve the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
Send at least 1 wei of collateral token to PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP contract and the `PerpetualAtlanticVault::settle` would be broken.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace `==` with `>=` or `<=` as appropriate.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/amo/UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol#L88


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The presence of the hardcoded router address can lead to token lockup issues when the contract is deployed on networks with a non-standard Uniswap router. Tokens sent to the contract for swapping purposes may not be routed correctly, potentially resulting in funds being locked in the protocol forever. This can result in users losing access to their tokens and can have severe financial consequences for affected users and the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
The contract contains the following line of code with the hardcoded router address:
univ3_router = ISwapRouter(0xE592427A0AEce92De3Edee1F18E0157C05861564);

The hardcoded address "0xE592427A0AEce92De3Edee1F18E0157C05861564" points to a specific instance of the Uniswap Router contract. In a situation where the contract is deployed on networks with a different Uniswap router address, token swaps may not function as intended. This can result in tokens becoming locked in the protocol, leaving users unable to withdraw their tokens except for ETH and protocol own token dpxETH.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

To ensure compatibility and flexibility across different networks, it is recommended to implement a more dynamic approach for setting the router address. Instead of hardcoding the router address, the contract should allow the router address to be set through a function mechanism for the contract owner to update the router address.

The recommendation is made in area of implementing an administrative function that allows the contract owner to update the router address after deployment. Ensure that only the contract owner can access and execute this function to prevent unauthorized changes.

## Impact
Storage variable `totalWethDelegated` can be easily manipulated if malicious user deposit big amount of weth and than imidieatly withdraw through `withdraw` functions. When normal user deposit weth they call `addToDelegate` function and deposited amount is added to `totalWethDelegated`: [totalWethDelegated += _amount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L964). The storage variable `totalWethDelegated` can be easily manipulated if a malicious user deposits a large amount of WETH and immediately withdraws it through the `withdraw` function. When a normal user deposits WETH, they call the `addToDelegate` function, and the deposited amount is added to `totalWethDelegated`: [totalWethDelegated += _amount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L964). # Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L123


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Liquidity providers can get zero shares when they deposit into PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.

## Proof of Concept
In deposit(), we first check if `(shares = previewDeposit(assets)) != 0`, and then we call perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding().

In updateFunding(), perpetualAtlanticVault will transfer funding into the PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP in a drip-vested manner, which will call addProceeds():

```solidity
  function addProceeds(uint256 proceeds) public onlyPerpVault {
    require(
      collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) >= _totalCollateral + proceeds,
      "Not enough collateral token was sent"
    );
    _totalCollateral += proceeds;
  }
```

As we can see, **_totalCollateral is increased. So the `assets.mulDivDown(supply, totalVaultCollateral)` in `convertToShares` is possible to round down to zero now. Especially when updateFunding transfers a lots funding into the PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.**

## Tools Used
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Reverse the order:

```solidity
    perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding();
    
    // Check for rounding error since we round down in previewDeposit.
    require((shares = previewDeposit(assets)) != 0, "ZERO_SHARES");

```


## Assessed type

Math

issues.body:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1195-L1198
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L919-L922
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L855-L858


# Vulnerability details

## Summary 
A premium is charged on $WETH when users simply `bond` or `bondWithDelegates`. This premium, however, is calculated twice in both of these functions and at two different points during execution. At those two points, the oracle is queried each time and no checks exist to make sure the returned price is the same during execution thus opening up the possibility of an oracle manipulation exploit.

## Impact
This can lead to inconsistencies in bond prices and invariants such as the premium and strike price being violated since the Oracle price returned is used to calculate these values. Malicious users can exploit this even further to cause the protocol financial loss.

## Proof of Concept
When the user calls `bond` or `bondWithDelegates`, `calculateBondCost` is also called to find the amount of RDPX and WETH required to bond.
- [bond()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L904)
```
 // Compute the bond cost
    (uint256 rdpxRequired, uint256 wethRequired) = calculateBondCost(
      _amount,
      rdpxBondId
    );
```

- [bondWithDelegates()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L705)
```
 (uint256 rdpxRequired, uint256 wethRequired) = calculateBondCost(
      _amount,
      rdpxBondId
    );
```
In `calculateBondCost`, the price oracle of RDPX is queried and the result is used for calculating the strike price, the rdpxRequired and a Premium which is then added to the amount of WETH required. This is the first time the Premium is calculated.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L669

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

rdpxRequiredInWeth / rdpxAmountInWeth calculation should use division instead of multiplication.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
    uint256 rdpxRequiredInWeth = (_rdpxRequired * getRdpxPrice()) / 1e8;

    uint256 rdpxAmountInWeth = (_rdpxAmount * getRdpxPrice()) / 1e8;

    /**
    * @notice Returns the price of rDPX against ETH
    * @dev    Price is in 1e8 Precision
    * @return rdpxPriceInEth rDPX price in ETH
    **/
    function getRdpxPrice() public view returns (uint256) {
      return
        IRdpxEthOracle(pricingOracleAddresses.rdpxPriceOracle)
          .getRdpxPriceInEth();
    }
```

getRdpxPrice returns the rDPX/WETH price. Calculating the rDPX quantity corresponding to the WETH quantity should be `rDPXAmount * 1e8 / getRdpxPrice()` instead of `_rdpxAmount * getRdpxPrice() / 1e8`.
Errors in calculations result in meaningless bondAmount result and disrupt internal accounting systems.
During the transfer, the wrong rdpxAmountInWeth will be calculated again.

## Tools Used

Manual review

Use the correct calculation formula

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L382
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L373


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`getLpTokenBalanceInWeth()` will return incorrect value.
Because if precision of `getLpPrice()` is `1e18`  then ```(lpTokenBalance * getLpPrice())``` in  `getLpTokenBalanceInWeth()` should be divided by 1e18 as the number of decimals in a LP token are `1e18`.
## Vulnerability Detail

```solidity
  function getLpPrice() public view returns (uint256) {
    // @audit here getLpPriceInEth's precision is not 1e8 its 1e18
    return IRdpxEthOracle(addresses.rdpxOracle).getLpPriceInEth();
  }
```

1. In `UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol` contract's `getLpPrice()` function it is assumed that the precision `getLpPriceInEth()` function of `RdpxEthOracle` is `1e8` but the actual precision of that function is `1e18`.

2. Due to this false assumption instead of dividing `(lpTokenBalance * getLpPrice())` by `1e18` they are dividing it by `1e8` in `getLpTokenBalanceInWeth()` function.

3. Due to this `getLpTokenBalanceInWeth()` precision will `1e28` but the precision of actual `WETH` token is `1e18`

```solidity
  function getLpTokenBalanceInWeth() external view returns (uint256) {
    return (lpTokenBalance * getLpPrice()) / 1e8;
  }
```


## Tools Used
   Manual Review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
If the return value of `getLpPrice()` needs to be in `1e8` precision divide the return value by `1e10` before returning.



## Assessed type

Decimal

Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

The strike price which is meant at to be at 25% below current price. However, when calculated with the roundUp function, exposes option writers to higher financial obligations.

The use of a roundUp function for setting the strike price can result in the strike price being significantly higher than if the value was simply truncated or rounded up. This discrepancy could lead to additional obligations for the option writer.

The formula currentPrice - (currentPrice / 4), which is 431,700 - 431,700/4 = 323,775( denoting 25% below current price)

However, with the roundUp Function: the formular uint256 remainder = _strike % roundingPrecision; 

uint 256 remainder = 323,775, since it is not zero it passes the check and returns  _strike - remainder + roundingPrecision which is 323,775-323,775+1000000

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/reLP/ReLPContract.sol#L233


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
More rdpx is removed, and the price will go higher than intended. In extreme situations where _amount is big enough (msg.sender has enough rdpx and eth), tokenAToRemove will be bigger than tokenALpReserve, then lpToRemove >totalSupply, revert the transaction.

## Proof of Concept
In the official doc: https://dopex.notion.site/rDPX-V2-RI-b45b5b402af54bcab758d62fb7c69cb4#23161c577fd1449085436e5a601358ae. We calculate the 
rDPX to remove as:  `((amount_lp * 4) / rdpx_supply) * lp_rdpx_reserves * base_relp_percent`.

However, in reLP(), we calculate the rdpx to remove as:
```solidity
uint256 tokenAToRemove = ((((_amount * 4) * 1e18) /
      tokenAInfo.tokenAReserve) *  // <------
      tokenAInfo.tokenALpReserve *
      baseReLpRatio) / (1e18 * DEFAULT_PRECISION * 1e2);
```

As we can see, we used tokenAInfo.tokenAReserve (IRdpxReserve(addresses.tokenAReserve).rdpxReserve(); // rdpx reserves) instead of the rdpx supply. This leads to a smaller divisor and bigger tokenAToRemove.

## Tools Used
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace `tokenAInfo.tokenAReserve` with `IERC20WithBurn(tokenA).totalSupply()`.

issues.title: The use of mulDivDown in _convertToAssets can result in small rounding errors over time that could lead to losses if shares are over-minted.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L226-L227


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Over many deposits/redeems, this discrepancy can accumulate and result in losses if more shares are minted than backed by assets.

## Proof of Concept
the use of mulDivDown in _convertToAssets can lead to small rounding errors over time that could result in losses if shares are over-minted.
Here is how it works:
The _convertToAssets function calculates the assets and rdpxAmount for a given number of shares like this: https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L226-L227
mulDivDown rounds down the result of the multiplication and division. So for example:
10 * 100 / 3 = 333.33 But mulDivDown(10, 100, 3) = 333
Over time, these small rounding errors can accumulate if new shares are minted based on the rounded down assets.
For example, say we have:
totalCollateral = 1000 supply = 100 shares = 10
_convertToAssets(10) would return: assets = 10 * 1000 / 100 = 100 (rounded down from 100.1)
Now if we deposit those 100 assets, we would mint:
sharesToMint = assets * supply / totalCollateral
= 100 * 100 / 1000 = 10
But the actual assets were 100.1, so we are minting slightly less shares than we should.



## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
Use mulDiv instead of mulDivDown, which will round to the nearest number instead of always rounding down.


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: the beforeWithdraw check does not properly account for potential losses in the vault. This could allow larger withdrawals than are safe.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L286-L302


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User could withdraw more assets than are actually available if there were unaccounted losses.

## Proof of Concept
 the beforeWithdraw check does not properly account for potential losses in the vault. This could allow larger withdrawals than are safe.

The beforeWithdraw check only looks at _totalCollateral and _activeCollateral to determine available collateral:
However, this does not account for any losses that may have occurred in the vault. The vault could have lost funds, but _totalCollateral would not have been updated to reflect that yet.

So a user could withdraw more assets than are actually available if there were unaccounted losses.

For example:
- Initial _totalCollateral = 100 ETH
- User deposits 10 ETH, _totalCollateral = 110 ETH
- Vault suffers a loss of 50 ETH. Actual collateral left is 60 ETH.
- But _totalCollateral is still 110 ETH
- User tries to withdraw 80 ETH. totalAvailableCollateral() returns 110 - 0 = 110 ETH
- Withdrawal of 80 ETH is allowed, even though only 60 ETH exists


## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
This could be mitigated by having totalAvailableCollateral() incorporate the vault's actual asset balance rather than relying solely on _totalCollateral.


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: DoS with donation to break strict equality `subtractLoss()`
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L201


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`subtractLoss()` is using strict equality in the require statement, which could easily be broke if malicious user donate 1 wei of collateral to the contract. `subtractLoss()` will be forever inoperable, and all future settlement calling this function will DoS.


## Proof of Concept

When `settle()` options, `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#subtractLoss()` will be called. And there is a require statement checks that the collateral balance is exactly `_totalCollateral - loss`.
```solidity
File: contracts\perp-vault\PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol
315:   function settle(
316:     uint256[] memory optionIds
317:   )

359:     IPerpetualAtlanticVaultLP(addresses.perpetualAtlanticVaultLP).subtractLoss(
360:       ethAmount
361:     );

File: contracts\perp-vault\PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol
199:   function subtractLoss(uint256 loss) public onlyPerpVault {
200:     require(
201:       collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss,
202:       "Not enough collateral was sent out"
203:     );
204:     _totalCollateral -= loss;
205:   }
```

The strict equality check is dangerous since malicious user can donate some amount of collateral to the contract to break the equality, even as little as 1 wei. Then `subtractLoss()` will DoS forever, making settlement impossible.

And there is no other way to adjust the balance error, currently all the `_totalCollateral` changes are tied to read balance change (deposit/withdraw/addProceeds, etc). 


## Tools Used
Manual analysis.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

- Use ">=" like `addRdpx()`.
- Or add some function to absorb the extra balance for collateral.




## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

issues.title: Extra balance withdrawn from `_transfer()` in RdpxV2Core causes unexpected reserve imbalance
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L677-L679


# Vulnerability details

### Impact
More than expected tokens are transfered from the `IRdpxReserve(addresses.rdpxReserve)` contract, which may lead to future calls to `_transfer()` to revert.

### POC
According to the logic provided in the contract spec, namely, the diagram in [SPEC](https://dopex.notion.site/rDPX-V2-RI-b45b5b402af54bcab758d62fb7c69cb4), users will provide RDPX and ETH in a ratio of 25% to 75% during regular bonding. The user-provided RDPX is burned (matching lines [656-659](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L656-L659)) or distributed to veDPX holders (matching lines [661-666](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L661-L666)). Then, a discount is computed (matching lines [670-674](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L670-L674)) and that discount is supposed to be sent from the reserves, as demonstrated by the "Send discount value in RDPX" arrow on the [diagram](https://dopex.notion.site/rDPX-V2-RI-b45b5b402af54bcab758d62fb7c69cb4) provided in the spec. However, instead of just sending the discount value, the reserve contract sends the entire amount of user-provided RDPX ___in addition to___ the discount value on lines [677-684](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L677-L684). This is inconsitent with the spec, and may lead to the reserve contract being drained of RDPX.

### Recommended Mitigation
Modify lines 677-684 such that only the discount value is withdrawn from the reserve contracts.


## Assessed type

Context

issues.title: the totalSupply of the UniswapV2Pair contract can potentially be manipulated, which could affect the amount of LP tokens removed in the reLP function.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/reLP/ReLPContract.sol#L237-L239


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This would drain extra LP tokens from the AMO

## Proof of Concept
Here lpToRemove depends on totalLpSupply. An attacker who controls the UniswapV2Pair contract could artificially increase totalSupply before this code runs. This would make lpToRemove larger than intended.
More LP tokens would be transferred from the AMO than needed. This could drain funds from the AMO.
To exploit this, an attacker would need to:
1. Deploy a malicious UniswapV2Pair contract that allows artificially setting totalSupply
2. Get the admin to set the addresses.pair to the malicious contract address
3. Call the reLP function
4. Manipulate totalSupply before lpToRemove is calculated



## Tools Used 
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
Calculate lpToRemove directly based on the actual reserves. This way lpToRemove depends only on the true reserves, not any potentially manipulated state. 


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/amo/UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol#L339-L346


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Low-level primitive `.call()` doesn't revert in caller's context when the callee reverts. If its return value is not checked, it can lead the caller to falsely believe that the call was successful. `UniV3LiquidityAMO.sol` uses `.call()` to transfer the native token to the receiver. If the receiver reverts, this can lead to locked tokens in UniV3LiquidityAMO.
contract
## Proof of Concept

````solidity
  function execute(
    address _to,
    uint256 _value,
    bytes calldata _data
  ) external onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) returns (bool, bytes memory) {
    (bool success, bytes memory result) = _to.call{ value: _value }(_data);
    return (success, result);
  }
````
## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Check the return value and revert if false is returned.
````diff
       (bool success, bytes memory result) = _to.call{ value: _value }(_data);
+      require(success);
````

## Impact
If the value of the slippage protection variable `minAmountOut` (the exact name of each slippage protection variable is attached to the submission) is `0`, then slippage protection is disabled and lots of tokens will be lost in `swaps` because of `MEV` and sandwich attacks.

Across several files that are in scope for the audit, there are numerous functions utilizing `swap` functions (provided by UniSwap and Curve) in different contexts as part of their function logic. In all these functions `swap` is used for exchanging tokens. All these functions have an argument `minAmountOut` (the argument name differs in different functions; each specific agrument name is attached to the submission), which is used as slippage protection for the `swap` function. The issue is that `minAmountOut`'s value is never checked inside functions and it is directly passed to the corresponding `swap` function. This presents a security threat, because calling a function with wrong arguments is not that uncommon. # Vulnerability details

## Impact
subtractLoss, which is called in the perpetualAtlanticVault when settling options, requires that the balance of the lp is equal to the collateral - loss. However, if anyone makes a donation attack of even 1 wei, this condition will not be true, leading to this condition always being true.

As a result of options not being settled, they will be worthless in terms of collateralization as they cannot ever be exercised.

Assume the balance of the lp is 100e18, collateral is 101e18 and loss is 1e18. An attacker sends 1 wei of collateral to the lp so that the balance is now 100e18 + 1. When the option is settled, now balance != colalteral - loss so the require statement fails and the option is not settled.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the condition to `collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) >= _totalCollateral - loss`

issues.title: Purchase function of vault lacks collateral but never sends it to the lp vault
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L255

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The purchase function of the perpetualAtlanticVault locks collateral but never sends the tokens to the lp. However the settle function does transferFrom the tokens from the lp. As a result, the vault will progressively siphon funds from the lp until tokens run out from the lp and a DoS results, as well as users losing their lp deposits.

## Proof of Concept
Assume lp has 100e18 collateral. Then vault makes a 100e18 deposit, locking 100e18 of collateral and preventing users from withdrawing this amount. Users who made deposits are now unable to withdraw their collateral. When later calling settle, the 100e18 collateral is transferred from the lp to the vault, draining the lp completely and leaving the vault with 100e18 collateral that is inaccessible. If another deposit / settle is made later on, the settle will fail due to the lp not having any tokens to transfer to the lp, resulting in DoS.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In addition to locking the collateral in the vault, transfer it to the lp as well.


## Assessed type

ERC20

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `RdpxV2Core.getRdpxPrice()` function is used to return the price of rDPX against ETH. The value returned by the `RdpxV2Core.getRdpxPrice()` is of very high importance since it is used for calculations in critical functions such as `RdpxV2Core._transfer()`, `RdpxV2Core.calculateBondCost()`, and `RdpxV2Core._calculateAmounts`. And those functions are used in main protocol use case implemented in the bonding functions such as `RdpxV2Core.bondWithDelegate()` and `RdpxV2Core.bond()`. 

The issue here is that the `RdpxV2Core` contract functions treat the value returned from the `getRdpxPrice` function to be in 1e8 precision as mentioned in its Natspec comments. But the returned value is actually in 1e18 precision. The `getRdpxPriceInEth` function is implemented in the `RdpxEthOracle` contract and its function implementation upgrades the precision to 1e18 before value is returned as shown below:

        price = consult(token0, 1e18);

Hence all the critical functions which use the return value of `getRdpxPrice` use the wrong precision for their calculations thus breaking the accounting of the entire protocol.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1051-L1070

# Vulnerability details

When the sequencer is down on Arbitrum state changes can still happen on L2 by passing them from L1 through the delayed inbox.
Dopex oracles may have stale prices, since L2-submitted transactions will not be processed.
It should always be checked before consuming any data from oracles.

## Impact
* If DpxETH were to de-peg while the sequencer is offline, stale price is used and can result incorrect `lowerDepeg` or `upperDepeg`
* Incorrect strike prices

## Proof of Concept
For example, Arbitrum sequencer is down:
1. DpxETH/ETH oracle stale price de-peg upper `1e8`, but real-time curve pool was de-peg lower `1e8`.
2. `upperDepeg` called and `DpxETH` reserves swap to `WETH`.
3. The Arbitrum sequencer came back and delayed transactions executed.
3. Swaps completed and `DpxETH` instead of peg, de-pegged(lower) more.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Check sequencer uptime before consuming any price data.
Read more: https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/l2-sequencer-feeds


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: Malicious user can escape from loss in case of settlement
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L315-L369
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L145-L175


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP share holder can front-run settlement and withdraw his funds from available collateral to escape loss after settlement.
## Vulnerability Details
when a new option is created required collateral for settlement has been locked in PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP , although this ensures full settlement but malicious user can front-run settlement and withdraw from available collateral of PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP and escape loss , this loss amount is added to other vault share holders loss.
## Impact
Malicious user escape from loss and add to vault share holders loss 
## Proof of Concept
Consider a scenario that there are 100 collateral and 10 shares in a PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP , 50 of collateral has been locked for settle option positions if required , and a user holds 5 shares in this vault. 
1 - an option hits strike price and admin calls settle function . 
2 - as 50 collateral is available in vault , malicious user front-runs settlement and withdraw 50 collateral ( for 5 shares ) , malicious user exited contract without loss 
3 - then settlement happens and loss for other vault share holders doubles . 
## Tools Used
Manual Review

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/reLP/ReLPContract.sol#L202


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

**Background info**

In `RDPX V2 FOR THE MENTALLY CHALLENGED` (https://blog.dopex.io/articles/dopex-papers/rdpx-v2-for-the-mentally-challenged) the CEO of the protocol said:

> V2 will be accompanied by **a permissioned rDPX/ETH AMM that will only accept deposits by the rDPX Treasury** and will have added sales tax for $rDPX sales. The treasury will pair $rDPX with $ETH to provide liquidity, allowing traders to swap $rDPX for $ETH as they desire.

However, that statement is an incorrect assumption.

What devs did, was to create a custom `Uniswap Router` that only accepts calls by the treasury.

But users/attackers can still directly interact with the uniswap pool, bypassing their `router`.

And by "interact", we mean *manipulate the balance and reserves of the pool*.

----

**The Vulnerable Implementation**

In `ReLPContract.sol` the `reLP(...)` function is called by the `RdpxV2Core.sol` smart contract, somewhere inside the `bond(...) ` and `bondWithDelegate(...)` functions.

This `reLP(...)` function (https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/reLP/ReLPContract.sol#L202):

1- Reads the reserves from a permissionless Uniswap pool.
2- Does some calculations with those values for slippage control.
3- Removes all liquidity
4- Adds the liquidity again.

We can manipulate the liquidity in the pool by swapping or adding more liquidity.

## Proof-of-Concept

**Example**

**Step 1**- Manipulate liquidity in the `rdpx/eth` pool
**Step 2**- Call `bond(...)` in `RdpxV2Core.sol`
**Step 3**- Manipulate liquidity in the `rdpx/eth` pool to make it go normal.

## Tools Used
Manual Review 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1. Create a permissioned rDPX/ETH AMM that will only accept deposits by the rDPX Treasury

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol `removeLiquidity()`, calls to UniswapV3 NonFungiblePositionManager is set with a deadline as `block.timestamp`. This is too restrictive for Arbitrum, and will most likely cause transactions to revert. 

Key liquidity management operations are going to be mostly unavailable. 

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
//UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol
  function removeLiquidity(
    uint256 positionIndex,
    uint256 minAmount0,
    uint256 minAmount1
  ) public onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) {
...
    INonfungiblePositionManager.DecreaseLiquidityParams
      memory decreaseLiquidityParams = INonfungiblePositionManager
        .DecreaseLiquidityParams(
          pos.token_id,
          liquidity,
          minAmount0,
          minAmount1,
|>        block.timestamp
        );
...
}
```
(https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol#L243-L251)
As seen above, `block.timestamp` is set as deadline for the call. According to arbitrum [doc](https://docs.arbitrum.io/faqs/misc-faqs), "Solidity calls to block.timestamp on Arbitrum are not linked to the timestamp of the L1 block, it is updated every L2 block based on the sequencer’s clock". And L2 block is "typically updated roughly every second". From abriscan, we see that each L2 block typically contains 2 or 3 or more transactions. See this [block](https://arbiscan.io/block/128273923) as an example.

As a result, this transaction will mostly revert. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Increase the deadline to `block.timestamp + 10` as an example.

The liquidity providers deposit `WETH` into the `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP` which in turn provides the required collateral for put options writing. Once a put is *in the money* it can be exercised by the `RdpxCoreV2` contract, which forces the liquidity providers to take on `rdpx` at above market prices (i.e. they take a loss).

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L125


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `RdpxV2Core` contract is using the `openzeppelin` `AccessControl` abstract contract for role based access control management of the contract. The `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` role which is the key role in the `RdpxV2Core` contract controls critical functions of the protocol.

This role (`DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`) is set to deployer of the `RdpxV2Core` contract inside its constructor as shown below:

    _setupRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, msg.sender); 

The issue here is that there is no option to change the account (`contract deployer account`) of `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` later if the account gets compromised in the future. 

There is a function in the `openzeppelin` `AccessControl.sol` contract to revoke the role from the existing account and grant it to a new account address as shown below:

    function revokeRole(bytes32 role, address account) public virtual override onlyRole(getRoleAdmin(role)) {

    function grantRole(bytes32 role, address account) public virtual override onlyRole(getRoleAdmin(role)) {

But as shown above these two functions can only be called by the `role`'s admin role. But the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` role is not configured with an admin role address in the `RdpxV2Core` contract. Hence above two functions to revoke and grant role to a new account address can not be called.

Hence the only way to remove the compromised `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` role account address would be to call the `AccessControl.renounceRole` function. Only the account with the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` can call this function. And the compromised account itself can only call this function and get removed from the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` role. If the `account address` with the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` was compromised then the attacker himself can call this function and remove the account address from the role.

Hence this will freeze the entire `RdpxV2Core` contract

issues.title: The token2AmountOutMin parameter alone is not sufficient to fully protect against price slippage in the swap function
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L304-L355


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users ends up with less token2 than expected due to the price change.

## Proof of Concept
The token2AmountOutMin parameter is supposed to protect against price slippage. But if the price moves unfavorably between approving the router and executing the swap, it could result in getting back less than expected. 
The token2AmountOutMin parameter alone is not sufficient to fully protect against price slippage in the swap function.
Here is how it works:
1. The swap function first transfers token1Amount of token1 from the rdpxV2Core contract to this contract using safeTransferFrom.
2. It then approves the router to spend token1Amount of token1.
3. The swap is executed on the router, specifying token2AmountOutMin as the minimum amount of token2 to receive.
The vulnerability is that between steps 2 and 3, the price could move unfavorably, resulting in getting back less token2 than expected.
For example:
• The swap is for 100 token1 to get back at least 95 token2 (token2AmountOutMin = 95).
• At the time of approval, 100 token1 is worth 100 token2.
• But by the time the swap executes, the price has moved and 100 token1 is only worth 90 token2.
• The swap will still go through since 90 > 95 token2AmountOutMin.
• But you end up with less token2 than expected due to the price change.


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
An additional check should be added after the swap to ensure the received token2 amount meets the original expected rate


## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L118
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L118


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP's `deposit` function is vulnerable to a cross-function re-entrancy that'll allow users to execute `redeem` during the following ERC777 transfer call:
```
function deposit(
    uint256 assets,
    address receiver
  ) public virtual returns (uint256 shares) {
   ...
   // Need to transfer before minting or ERC777s could reenter.
   collateral.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), assets);
```

`redeem` can be called during a [tokensToSend](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/2.x/api/token/erc777#IERC777Sender) callback where a user can receive RDPX tokens and PerpetaulAtlanticVault LP Tokens with their collateral transferred back. 

## Proof of Concept

1. Execute `deposit(uint256 assets, address = attacker contract)` to mint some shares first. 
1. Execute `deposit(uint256 assets, address = attacker contract)` again.
2. `collateral.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), assets)` triggers `tokensToSend` callback. PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP gets user's collateral.
3. Execute `redeem(previewDeposit(assets), receiver = attacker, owner = attacker)` in the callback.
4. User's PerpetaulAtlanticVault LP tokens get burned. The attacker gets `rdpx` tokens and his collateral back. 
5. The callback completes and new PerpetaulAtlanticVault LP Tokens are minted in `deposit`. 
6. `_totalCollateral` is unchanged. `_totalCollateral + assets - assets = _totalCollateral`.

In the end, the user receives RDPX and PerpetaulAtlanticVault LP Tokens without putting down a collateral.

## Tools Used
Manual Analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add OpenZeppelin's reentrancyguard to both `deposit` and `redeem`.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L283


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Liquidity can be drained 

## Proof of Concept
The key parts of the code:
1. In removeLiquidity(), the router is only approved to remove lpAmount:https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L268
2. Then removeLiquidity is called on the router:https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L271-L280
3. After this returns, lpTokenBalance is updated:https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L283
The vulnerability is that a malicious actor could:
A. See the approve transaction in the mempool
B. Quickly create their own removeLiquidity transaction with a higher lpAmount
C. If they are able to get their transaction mined before the original one, they could drain more liquidity than intended
This is because the router is approved to remove more tokens than intended.


## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The contract should approve the router for the maximum possible amount before calling removeLiquidity. This way, the router is approved for the maximum amount, preventing front-running attacks.The lpTokenBalance should also be updated before calling removeLiquidity to prevent removing more than the balance

issues.title: Incorrect shares calculation in `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.deposit`
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L123-L125


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.deposit` function looks like this:
```solidity
  function deposit(
    uint256 assets,
    address receiver
  ) public virtual returns (uint256 shares) {
    require((shares = previewDeposit(assets)) != 0, "ZERO_SHARES");
    perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding();
    ...
  }
```
It can be seen that the shares amount for the deposit is calculated before performing the `perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding`, which is incorrect.

The `perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding` function sends collateral tokens to the vaultLp contract and hence updates `_totalCollateral` value.

The incorrect execution order of the above mentioned statements causes loss of funds for the contract.


## Proof of Concept
- Collateral tokens in vaultLp is 100 and supply is 100.
- An attacker observes that the next `updateFunding` call will send 10 tokens to vaultLp.
- Attacker invokes the `deposit` function with 100 as input. His shares is calculated as 100. After that `updateFunding` is executed and 10 collateral tokens get transferred to vaultLp.
- Attacker receives 100 shares tokens.
- Now the contract has 210 collateral tokens (100 + 10 + 100) and 200 shares supply.
- Instantly, the attacker calls `redeem` and receives back 105 collateral tokens.

The attack caused instant profit of 5 tokens to the attacker, profit can be increased by increasing the attacker deposit amount. If attacker deposits 10k tokens he can capture all the additional 10 tokens.

This bug also leads to a scenario in which two depositors receive different ratio of shares even when they deposit in the same block.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Calculate the shares after performing the `updateFunding`.


## Assessed type

Context

## Description
The value obtained from ```rdpxReserve()``` will indirectly determine a rate between the bonding amount and lp amount to remove from the UniV2Amo contract. 
As the bonding amount correlates directly with ```rdpx``` and ```weth``` amounts, this setup would halt the protocol from earning income to maintain its peg, whenever ```isReLPActive``` is set to true.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/reLP/ReLPContract.sol#L228-L237


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

ReLPContract.reLP uses the state of the uniswap pool instead of internal state when calculating lpToRemove, which is wrong.
Users may directly inject funds into the pool to make the market, or malicious users may frontrun to inject funds, which may lead to reLP DOS.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
    (uint256 reserveA, uint256 reserveB) = UniswapV2Library.getReserves(
      addresses.ammFactory,
      tokenASorted,
      tokenBSorted
    );

    // get tokenA reserves
    tokenAInfo.tokenAReserve = IRdpxReserve(addresses.tokenAReserve)
      .rdpxReserve(); // rdpx reserves

    tokenAInfo.tokenALpReserve = addresses.tokenA == tokenASorted
      ? reserveA
      : reserveB;

    uint256 baseReLpRatio = (reLPFactor *
      Math.sqrt(tokenAInfo.tokenAReserve) *
      1e2) / (Math.sqrt(1e18)); // 1e6 precision

    uint256 tokenAToRemove = ((((_amount * 4) * 1e18) /
      tokenAInfo.tokenAReserve) *
      tokenAInfo.tokenALpReserve *
      baseReLpRatio) / (1e18 * DEFAULT_PRECISION * 1e2);

    uint256 totalLpSupply = IUniswapV2Pair(addresses.pair).totalSupply();

    uint256 lpToRemove = (tokenAToRemove * totalLpSupply) /
      tokenAInfo.tokenALpReserve;
```

Analyzing from a mathematical formula, it is assumed that users directly add and double the liquidity to the pool.
The `reserveA` and `reserveB` (`tokenALpReserve`) will be doubled, `tokenAReserve` remains unchanged,`baseReLpRatio` remains unchanged, `tokenAToRemove` will be doubled, and `totalLpSupply` will be doubled, so `lpToRemove` will be doubled.
That is, if the user directly injects funds into the pool, the calculated `lpToRemove` will become larger. When `lpToRemove` is greater than the lp actually owned by amo, the reLP execution will revert. Below is the POC used for testing:

issues.title: PerpetualAtlanticVault.settle() may be DoSed by attacker.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L201


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
PerpetualAtlanticVault can not be settled forever.

## Proof of Concept
When an attacker transfers few amount of collateral token to `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP`, the function - 'PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#substractLoss' is always reverted because `real balance` is different from the value - `_totalCollateral`.

PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#substractLoss is following.
```solidity
File: PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol
199:   function subtractLoss(uint256 loss) public onlyPerpVault {
200:     require(
201:       collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss,
202:       "Not enough collateral was sent out"
203:     );
204:     _totalCollateral -= loss;
205:   }
```
In L201, the equation `collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss` is based on the assumption in which `collateral.balanceof(address(this))` is always synced with `_totalCollateral`.

But an attacker transfers few amount of collateral token to `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP` contract, this assumption becomes wrong.

Then, this function is always reverted.

On the other hand, the function - `PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#settle` calls this function - `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#substractLoss`.

So, in this case, function - `PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#settle` is always reverted.

## Tools Used
Manual Review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```solidity
File: PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol
199:   function subtractLoss(uint256 loss) public onlyPerpVault {
200:     require(
201: -     collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss,
201: +     collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) >= _totalCollateral - loss,
202:       "Not enough collateral was sent out"
203:     );
204:     _totalCollateral -= loss;
205:   }
```


## Assessed type

DoS

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L201


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.subtractLoss` function contains this validation statement
```solidity
  function subtractLoss(uint256 loss) public onlyPerpVault {
    require(
      collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalCollateral - loss,
      "Not enough collateral was sent out"
    );
    _totalCollateral -= loss;
  }
```
The function has a strict equality check for collateral token balance. Anyone can donate 1 wei to collateral token to the VaultLp contract and force this function to always revert.

Due to this the `PerpetualAtlanticVault.settle` function will also always revert. Hence no bond can be settled ever.

## Proof of Concept
- In PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP, the collateral token balance and `_totalCollateral` is 100.
- An attacker donates 1 wei of collateral tokens to the contract.
- In the next `settle` call, the balance of VaultLp is reduced by 10 and `subtractLoss` is invoked. But now the token balance of contract is 91 (100 + 1 - 10) and `_totalCollateral` is 100.
- The require statement reverts as `91 != 100 - 10`.
- `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.subtractLoss` reverts.
- `PerpetualAtlanticVault.settle` reverts.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `>=` operator instead of `==`.


## Assessed type

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Even when the dev deals with blacklisted addresses in the `emergencyWithdraw()` the blacklisted token will still be locked there, for this problem another address needs authorization to withdraw it when this happens.

## Proof of Concept
Suppose the owner needs to call `emergencyWithdraw()` but the sender is blacklisted from one specific token [another issue already reported by me], lets say that this issue was already fixed and the loop is now checking if the user and the contract are blacklisted by the current token `i` before transferring the tokens without reverting, it will then send all the allowed ones but not allowed will still remain in the contract stuck, for this reason a new function has be created for another address [admin controlled] can withdraw these tokens in an emergency case, or in any case really.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a new function so the owner can choose another address to withdraw the token since his address is blacklisted, if the backup address is chosen beforehand there can be the risk of the attacker also compromise it with tainted funds [from a mixer], so another option would be adding adding an address at the moment of the withdrawing. 

This will only work if the msg.sender was blacklisted, if it was the contract instead then even the attacker wont be able to withdraw these tokens.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In the `purchase()` function, the contract calculates the `requiredCollateral` needed for writing the option based on the `amount` and `strike` price. Subsequently, it checks whether this amount is less than or equal to the `totalAvailableCollateral` from `perpetualAtlanticVaultLp`. While this is a prudent step to ensure that the vault has enough collateral, there is a potential risk of a system halt or liquidity crisis if the check fails.

```
uint256 requiredCollateral = (amount * strike) / 1e8;
_validate(
  requiredCollateral <= perpetualAtlanticVaultLp.totalAvailableCollateral(),
  3
);
```
## Proof-of-Concept

If the liquidity pool does not have enough collateral, the smart contract will throw an error, halting the option-writing operation. This would have a cascading impact on the system’s overall liquidity and potentially result in failure to maintain the risk profile. Bonds would no longer be able to be purchased, LP shares would no longer be redeemed, and other issues may arise.

Dopex would have to turn off `putOptionsRequired` at minimum to keep bonding afloat. Hopefully the treasury is still collateralized

Manual Review

Implement a mechanism that dynamically adjusts collateral requirements based on the current risk

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L405-L459

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L419-L423
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L440-L449


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The totalFundingForEpoch mapping can record inflated total funding amounts for an epoch if options are double counted. This means more funding could be withdrawn from the protocol than required.

## Proof of Concept
The calculateFunding function can potentially double count funding amounts if the total option amounts or funding rates change between calls.

The issue is that it doesn't re-calculate the number of options to fund for the epoch. It uses optionsPerStrike[strike] - fundingPaymentsAccountedForPerStrike[latestFundingPaymentPointer][strike].

So if optionsPerStrike[strike] changes between calls, it could end up double counting options that were already funded in a previous call.

Similarly, if the funding rate changes, the new rate will be applied to options that were already funded at a previous rate.

This could result in the totalFundingForEpoch being larger than it should be.

## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
 calculateFunding should recalculate the total options to fund each call.  it avoids potential double counting issues if options amounts change between calls.


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: `PerpetualVaultLP::deposit` allots additional shares to depositors at the expense of existing LPs
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.sol#L123


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`PerpetualVaultLP::deposit` computes shares for the deposit using the `previewDeposit` function. `previewDeposit` calculates shares proportional to the assets deposited v/s the `totalCollateral` which is the sum of `ETH` and `RDPX` collateral.

Note that `perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding()` is called AFTER shares are computed. `updateFunding` has the effect of increasing `totalCollateral` as the vault gets the `funding fees` from the options it has written to `RdpxV2Core`. Since total collateral used for calculating shares does not include the funding fees, depositors end up with marginally additional shares at the expense of existing LP's. In effect, this is like stealing value from existing LP's and sharing it with new depositors.  

## Proof of Concept
1. Bob is an existing LP having all the supply (100 shares) against 1 ETH as total collateral
2. Funding accrued since last update is equal to 0.25 ETH
3. Pete deposits 0.25 ETH into the vault
4. As per current calculation, Pete gets 0.25*100/1.25 = 20 shares
5. Actual calculation should have been 0.25*100/ (1.25 + 0.25) = 16 shares (rounded)

Pete got 4 additional shares at the expense of Bob because Pete's share calculation does not include the collateral already accrued in the form of funding fees.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Call `perpetualAtlanticVault.updateFunding()` before calculating shares via `previewDeposit(assets)`


## Assessed type

ERC4626

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L978-L989


# Vulnerability details

Users can delegate WETH using `RdpxV2Core.addToDelegate(amount, fee)`. This will transfer `amount` WETH from the user to the core contract, and [add `amount` to the `totalWethDelegated` state variable](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L964).
Then, users can withdraw the unused WETH using `RdpxV2Core.withdraw(delegateId)`, which will transfer at most `amount` WETH back to the user, but [leaving `totalWethDelegated` unchanged](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L978-L989).

The big issue comes when `RdpxV2Core.sync()` is called, since it [deducts the incorrect `totalWethDelegated` from the WETH balance of the core contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1001-L1003), leaving `reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance` with an incorrect value, lower than it should really be. **This incorrect value is then used in many sensitive functions of the core contract**.

## Impact

Although the issue exists even when users use the protocol as intended, it becomes much more severe when an **attacker abuses it to arbitrarily reduce the "cached" WETH balance of the core contract** (i.e. `reserveAsset[reservesIndex["WETH"]].tokenBalance`).

> Note that the attacker does not need a big amount of ETH to execute this; they can either deposit and withdraw small amounts repeatedly (paying only the associated gas fees), or they can take a flash loan, deposit, withdraw and repay it in the same transaction.

This behavior will lead to a **DoS on critical functions of the core contract**, making them revert due to **Arithmetic underflow errors**. The affected functions in the core contract are:
- [`lowerDepeg(...)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.so

issues.title: The calculateBondCost function does not account for potential changes in parameters like bondMaturity and bondDiscountFactor between when it is called and when bond() is actually executed.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1156-L1199


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
- Users end up bonding at a cost that no longer matches the calculateBondCost return values
- Users ends up paying more than estimated due to the changed parameters.

## Proof of Concept
The calculateBondCost function does not account for potential changes in parameters like bondMaturity and bondDiscountFactor between when it is called and when bond() is actually executed. This could result in a mismatch between the estimated bond cost returned by calculateBondCost and the actual cost when bonding.
The key parameters that could change are:
•	bondMaturity - This affects the put option cost if putOptionsRequired is true. A shorter maturity means lower option cost.
•	bondDiscountFactor - This provides a discount on the rDPX portion of the bond cost. A higher factor means a larger discount.
If these parameters are changed to a lower value in between the calls, the actual bond cost would be higher than estimated by calculateBondCost.
For example:
1. User calls calculateBondCost() 
o    bondMaturity = 30 days
o    bondDiscountFactor = 10%
o    Returns: 1000 rDPX, 9000 ETH
2. Admin reduces bondMaturity to 7 days and bondDiscountFactor to 5%
3.   User calls bond() with 1000 rDPX and 9000 ETH 
o    Actual cost is now 1100 rDPX, 9100 ETH due to reduced maturity and discount
This means the user bondes with insufficient rDPX and ETH compared to the new parameters.


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
- calculateBondCost should read the current parameter values instead of hardcoded ones
- bond() should re-check the bond cost right before bonding and revert if insufficient funds were provided.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/main/contracts/amo/UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol#L332


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Eventhough the `RdpxV2Core` contract implements a ERC721Holder, allowing itself to receive ERC721 tokens, it has no functionality for managing them. For example, it does not include functions for transferring the tokens to other addresses, approving other addresses to manage the tokens, or checking the balance of tokens held by the contract.
For this reason, any ERC721 tokens which are `recoverERC721` to the `RdpxV2Core` will be stuck there forever. More severely, if the `NonfungiblePositionManager` NFTs managed by the `UniV3LiquidityAmo` were to withdrawn to the `RdpxV2Core`, the entire collateral committed to these NFTs can never be redeemed, resulting in a loss of funds.

```solidity
// Findings are labeled with '<= FOUND'
// File: contracts/amo/UniV3LiquidityAmo.sol
324:  function recoverERC721(
325:    ...
330:    INonfungiblePositionManager(tokenAddress).safeTransferFrom(
331:      address(this),
332:      rdpxV2Core, // <= FOUND: rdpxV2Core cannot handle ERC721s sent from UniV3LiquidityAmo
333:      token_id
334:    );
335:    emit RecoveredERC721(tokenAddress, token_id);
336:  }
```

## Proof of Concept

1. Alice, a system admin, attempts to `recoverERC721` an `ERC721` token to `rdpxV2Core`.

2. Since `rdpxV2Core` has no function to handle other types of ERC721 tokens, the "recovered" ERC721 token gets stuck in `rdpxV2Core` forever.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider sending the ERC721 token to a trusted address (`address _to`) that can handle all ERC721 tokens.

ERC721

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It disincentivizes usage of the rDPX decaying bonds, since there is no discount. Users would be better off just bonding directly with rDPX.

## Proof of Concept

This calculates the discount based on the square root of the rDPX reserve amount. The higher the reserve, the higher the discount.
However, when bonding with rDPX decaying bonds, there is no discount applied: https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1180-L1187 
This means users could get better rates by bonding directly with rDPX rather than rDPX decaying bonds.

Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
The discount logic should be made consistent between direct rDPX bonding and rDPX decaying bond bonding

issues.title: Wrong calculation in PerpetualAtlanticVault.calculateFunding() make the core contract sending more collateral than expected
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L405-L459


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `timeToExpiry` is calculated wrong in `PerpetualAtlanticVault.calculateFunding()`, make it calculate the premium price bigger than it should be, thus cost more funding

## Proof of Concept
The `timeToExpiry` is calculated like this:  
```solidity 
uint256 timeToExpiry = nextFundingPaymentTimestamp() - (genesis + ((latestFundingPaymentPointer - 1) * fundingDuration));
```
`nextFundingPaymentTimestamp()` is calculated like this:  
```solidity
return genesis + (latestFundingPaymentPointer * fundingDuration);
```
Based on this, `timeToExpiry` is obviously equals to `fundingDuration` which is bigger than expected. `timeToExpiry` should be the time range from now to the next funding payment timestamp.
And because of bigger `timeToExpiry` than expected, when we apply Black Scholes equation, we will get a bigger premium price than expected.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
- uint256 timeToExpiry = nextFundingPaymentTimestamp() - (genesis + ((latestFundingPaymentPointer - 1) * fundingDuration));
+ uint256 timeToExpiry = nextFundingPaymentTimestamp() - block.timestamp;
```








## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
- An attacker crashes the RDPX price
- The admin sets a high bond discount factor
- The high discount is applied evenly to the RDPX and ETH ratios
- So the attacker can bond large amounts of ETH while still needing to provide lots of cheap RDPX


## Proof of Concept
The way the discount factor is applied evenly to both the ETH and RDPX ratios when calculating the bond cost could potentially be problematic in certain situations.
The vulnerability arises because the discount is applied evenly to both the RDPX and ETH ratios, regardless of the relative prices.
For example, if the RDPX price crashed 90% below the ETH price. Applying a 50% discount evenly would still require a significant amount of RDPX to bond (25% of the original RDPX ratio). This doesn't make much sense, since RDPX is now very cheap compared to ETH.


## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Apply the discount proportionally based on the relative prices of RDPX and ETH.
